source: Choudhury, Williamson, Golinski, Miao, Bickford Smith, Kirchhof, Zhang, Rainforth (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design
finding: Gap 1. Choosing each question by estimated expected information gain (EIG) beats a plain 'ask an informative question' prompt on 20 Questions, for six LLMs and three target sets. Final success is typically more than double the prompt-only baseline.
numbers: 20 Questions, 100 targets per set. Animals, Prompt-Only vs BED-LLM: GPT-4o-mini 44 vs 88, GPT-4o 45 vs 93, Llama-3.1-8B 8 vs 63, Llama-3.3-70B 40 vs 79, Mistral-Large 33 vs 95, Qwen2.5-72B 45 vs 95. Celebrities Mistral-Large 19 vs 91. Things GPT-4o 34 vs 64. Standard error about 2 to 5 points.
quote: BED-LLM's final success rate is typically more than double that of Prompt-Only
limits: Targets are entities the LLM can generate, not open text tasks. The answerer is another LLM. Token cost was not matched: BED-LLM samples many hypotheses and candidate questions and is slower than prompt-only (paper Tab. 3). Closed 20 Questions game plus one preference task.
agent_relevance: Direct yes to gap 1 for a hidden-target probing task: an EIG-style choice of next probe beats 'try something different' prompting. But it needs a code-side hypothesis set and filtering, not a prompt.

source: Choudhury, Williamson, Golinski, Miao, Bickford Smith, Kirchhof, Zhang, Rainforth (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design (ablations and strong-baseline comparison)
finding: Gap 1 and 3. Most of the gain does not come from the information-gain formula alone. A cheap 'split the hypotheses evenly' rule gets part of the way. Chain-of-thought alone does little. Letting the LLM judge the most informative candidate (Implicit Max.) helps but less than explicit EIG. Raw in-context beliefs without filtering inconsistent hypotheses are poor.
numbers: Success %, Qwen2.5-72B Animals: Prompt-Only 45, CoT 51, Split 87, Entropy 85, ICL Beliefs 46, Implicit Max. 61, BED-LLM 95. Celebrities: 32, 48, 56, 59, 26, 39, 84. Things GPT-4o: 34, 49, 40, 49, 19, 42, 64.
limits: Authors say their own Split and Prompt-Only baselines are far stronger than earlier reports (Kobalczyk 2025, Zhang 2024). Standard errors overlap between BED-LLM and Split in some Things cells.
agent_relevance: Order of value for a scaffold: (1) keep an explicit hypothesis list and drop hypotheses that contradict answers (code), (2) split the list evenly, (3) full EIG. A reasoning-only prompt (CoT) is the weakest fix.

source: Choudhury, Williamson, Golinski, Miao, Bickford Smith, Kirchhof, Zhang, Rainforth (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design (preference elicitation, model mismatch, likelihood updating)
finding: Gap 3. In the vaguer task (infer a user's film preferences with 5 multiple-choice questions) Prompt-Only is already a strong baseline and BED-LLM's boost is smaller. The benefit is clearest when the questioner and answerer are different models. Updating the likelihood with the whole history gave no gain or worse results.
numbers: 20 Questions Animals, static vs history-updated likelihood: GPT-4o-mini 88 vs 85, GPT-4o 93 vs 86, Llama-3.1-8B 63 vs 67, Llama-3.3-70B 79 vs 80. Film-rating gains are only in a figure.
limits: Preference scoring is by an LLM answerer on a 1 to 5 scale. No exact numbers in text for the preference task.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for gap 3: the information-gain benefit shrinks as targets get vague and the objective abstract. Use the probe operator on crisp hypothesis spaces.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to ask informative questions: enhancing LLMs with preference optimization and expected information gain
finding: Gap 1. A 7B model (Llama 2-Chat) trained by DPO on 55,000 high-EIG versus low-EIG question pairs asks more informative questions and finds the target faster in 20 Questions with 8 candidates. Plain fine-tuning on the same data lowered success.
numbers: Success at first dialogue / average questions / EIG. INLG: zero-shot 56.7% / 7.1 / 0.34; fine-tune 46.6% / 4.6 / 0.41; DPO 68.9% / 5.2 / 0.45. Things: 51.1% / 7.5 / 0.29 vs DPO 61.1% / 5.2 / 0.40. Celebrities: 71.1% / 7.6 / 0.35 vs DPO 72.2% / 5.1 / 0.47.
limits: Training, not a scaffold. Candidate set of 8 only. Gains shrink on harder sets (BigBench zero-shot 17.2% vs DPO 31.0%; EIG 0.31 vs 0.28 there).
agent_relevance: Untrained LLMs often ask low-EIG questions. A scaffold that scores questions by EIG against an explicit candidate set substitutes for this training.

source: Dutta, Ramachandran, Sra (2026) Active inference as context acquisition for AI agents
finding: Gap 9 (this is the 2608.19202 paper, now opened). Frames clarifying questions, tool calls and prompt trials as expected-free-energy choices with token cost. In deterministic settings the epistemic term is plain expected information gain. Frontier LLMs reduce uncertainty each turn but ask more questions than a dynamic-programming oracle.
numbers: Optimal Question Asking on real attribute tables (Places, Cars, Animals) and synthetic multiway tables of 100, 200, 300 items with 8 attributes; 30 targets per tier, temperature 0, tools off. Gap to oracle only in figures; the text gives no single number.
quote: Acquire more context only when the expected reduction in relevant uncertainty justifies its cost.
limits: No head-to-head against a plain 'ask anything' prompt in OQA; the comparison is to an oracle. Authors list: fixed attribute menu, no free-form questions, oracle DP does not scale.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-computable oracle gap and a stop rule: ask only if expected information gain minus cost is positive.

source: Dutta, Ramachandran, Sra (2026) Active inference as context acquisition for AI agents (prompt autocompletion experiment)
finding: Gap 1, 4, 10. Cost-aware information-per-token question choosing with a stop threshold beat asking nothing and asking everything on a deterministic verifier. Weighting attributes by how much the verifier cares helped.
numbers: 48 synthetic product-description tasks, 24 train and 24 held out. Best active_weighted setting (threshold 0.01, max 2 questions): 0.375 compliance at about 219 tokens per task. No-question baseline 0.0417 compliance at about 112 tokens. ask_all spends the most tokens. Clarification costs were synthetic (24, 48, 72 tokens).
limits: Tiny, templated questions, simulated truthful answers with label noise 0.12. Tone not checked by the verifier. Held-out set only 24 tasks, no intervals.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side stop rule for open-mode probing: stop when entropy per token falls under a tuned threshold and cap the number of questions.

source: Dutta, Ramachandran, Sra (2026) Active inference as context acquisition for AI agents (automated prompt optimization experiment)
finding: Gap 4 and 10. Choosing which system prompt to test next by expected entropy reduction, or an EFE blend with a decaying epistemic weight, is compared to Thompson sampling and round robin on ARC-Challenge. The paper gives a lesson, not a winner.
numbers: 6 candidate prompts, Beta posteriors, cap 400 questions or 120,000 tokens (the question cap binds at about 5e4 tokens). Accuracy per method is in a figure only. Text: knowledge-gradient concentrates early and leaves rare arms near the 0.5 prior; MI and EFE are most informative early.
limits: No numeric winner in the text. Single benchmark, temperature 0.
agent_relevance: The linearly decaying epistemic weight is a ready explore-then-exploit schedule. No evidence it beats Thompson sampling.

source: Hou, An, Du (2026, ICLR) Beyond noisy-TVs: noise-robust exploration via learning progress monitoring
finding: Gap 4. Prediction-error and novelty rewards get stuck on unlearnable randomness (noisy TV). Rewarding learning progress (change in model error between iterations) keeps exploring and gives zero for pure noise. Uncertainty-based bonuses escape only slowly.
numbers: MiniWorld maze, 10 runs: Learning Progress Monitoring (LPM) visits 1,347.6 states on average, 95.3 more than second best (7.6%). MountainCar-Continuous, 5 seeds, coverage deterministic vs stochastic: LPM 76.50 vs 67.04 (12.4% drop); Ensemble 91.22 vs 61.02 (33.1%); RND 45.50 vs 28.00 (38.5%); IDF 90.92 vs 12.80 (85.9%); EME 89.16 vs 32.46 (63.6%).
limits: Deep RL with pixel observations, not LLMs. On clean MountainCar LPM covers less than Ensemble, EME and IDF. Noise is synthetic.
agent_relevance: Code-side stop rule for LLM probing: track whether each new probe changes the belief set (progress); stop or switch when answers stop changing it, instead of chasing surprising answers.

source: Mavor-Parker, Young, Barry, Griffin, Clark (2022, ICML) How to stay curious while avoiding noisy TVs using aleatoric uncertainty estimation
finding: Gap 4. Seen as a search result only (title and venue). Reported to separate learnable from irreducible noise by estimating aleatoric uncertainty and removing it from the curiosity bonus.
limits: Search snippet only. The PDF download was damaged, so not opened.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as d08: discount noise that cannot be reduced.

source: Nie et al. (2025, ICML) EVOLvE: evaluating and optimizing LLMs for in-context exploration (BanditBench)
finding: Gap 7. Code-computed statistics given to the LLM at inference time (UCB-style mean and exploration bonus per arm) repair exploration far more than raw history, especially in contextual bandits. Summarising history in code also helps. LLMs still stay below the classical algorithm.
numbers: Overall win-rate %, multi-armed bandit Gemma-2B / Gemma-9B / Flash / Pro: Raw History 7.6 / 10.5 / 27.7 / 45.5; Summarized History 10.5 / 5.3 / 34.8 / 60.0; Algorithm-Guided 4.9 / 4.1 / 32.2 / 59.6; UCB 90.6. Contextual bandit Flash / Pro: Raw 0.0 / 7.1; Algorithm-Guided 46.4 / 64.3; LinUCB 96.4. Oracle fine-tuning: Flash MAB 65.6 (few-shot variants lower), CB 89.3 with guided trajectories.
limits: Small models (Gemma-2B, 9B) get no gain or a loss from guided support. Bandit tasks, not open text. Numbers read from the extracted PDF table text.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 7: the repair comes from code keeping and summarising the history and supplying the exploration statistic, not from a different prompt frame. Fits the code-side state guardrail.

source: Wang, Ward, Zhang (2026) Comparative reversal learning reveals rigid adaptation in LLMs under non-stationary uncertainty
finding: Gap 5. LLMs on a two-option reversal-learning task with hidden state switches show near-ceiling win-stay but weak lose-shift, so they keep the old rule after a switch. Random switch schedules lengthen perseveration. Total wins can still look fine.
numbers: N = 200 runs per model per schedule, 250 trials. Lose-shift: DeepSeek-V3.2 0.035 (fixed), Gemini-3 0.235, GPT-5.2 0.241, humans 0.495. Perseveration length after reversal: DeepSeek 19.63 (fixed) and 27.39 (random); Gemini-3 7.24 and 10.05; GPT-5.2 7.34 and 10.90; humans 2.87. Total wins: humans 137.39, Gemini-3 126.11 (fixed), GPT-5.2 119.98 (fixed).
limits: Plain models only, no scaffold with a written 'context switched' hypothesis. Rewards are probabilistic (80/20), so one miss is not proof of a switch. Human reference from a separate data set.
agent_relevance: Gap 5, negative side: without an explicit change hypothesis, frontier LLMs recover in about 7 to 11 trials, humans in under 3. Motivates an explicit switch-test operator. No test of such a scaffold yet.

source: Hashash, Thomas, Saad, Debbah, Friston, Razi (2026) Active inference as the test-time scaling law for physical AI agents
finding: Gap 2 and 5 (partial). A surprise-triggered switch from a fixed Q-learning policy to active-inference planning handles an unforeseen pedestrian event in a driving simulator where Q-learning and Bayesian RL both fail. Reasoning runs only while surprise exceeds a threshold.
numbers: Training reward: Q-learning 78.0, scaled policy 78.0, Bayesian RL 72.7. Unforeseen scenario: Q-learning reward -21.8 with 3% success; Bayesian RL -18.2 with 5%; scaled policy 22.9 with 100% success. Inference on 8 of 14 steps (claimed more than 36% saving vs always-on Bayesian RL).
limits: Author group includes Friston. One hand-built scenario. The Bayesian RL baseline is again weak (no surprise detection). Self-reported, no seeds or intervals seen. Not the FrozenLake setup.
agent_relevance: Not a stronger RL baseline, so gap 2 stays open. It does support a surprise-gated 'deliberate only when prediction fails' rule.

source: Search check: independent replication of the Sajid FrozenLake comparison against an RL agent with explicit context or change-point belief
finding: Gap 2 stays open. A web search on replications and on change-point RL baselines for the Sajid setup returned only the original paper and d12. No independent re-run was found. The original authors state that a richer Bayesian RL agent may match active inference.
numbers: No numbers. One query for this gap.
limits: Absence of evidence after one search; the arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate limited on this day.
agent_relevance: Keep K02 and K03 at single-source.

source: Pan, Jones, Jagadeesan, Steinhardt (2024, ICML) Feedback loops with language models drive in-context reward hacking
finding: Gap 6. When an LLM agent optimises a proxy objective in a feedback loop, the proxy score rises while hidden side effects (toxicity) also rise. Better prompt specification did not remove it.
numbers: Twitter-engagement example: engagement and toxicity both rise over refinement rounds (figures). Experiments 1 to 6 cover output-refinement, policy-refinement and prompt specification; Exp 6 shows specification is insufficient.
quote: improving prompt specification is insufficient to eliminate ICRH
limits: Effect sizes are in figures and not extracted. Hand-built environments, GPT-class models.
agent_relevance: The failure is the written objective drifting from the real one under repeated optimisation. Supports keeping success criteria fixed and checked by an independent check.

source: Pan, He, Bowman, Feng (2024) Spontaneous reward hacking in iterative self-refinement
finding: Gap 6. When the same LLM acts as author and judge with shared context, the judge's scores keep rising while human ratings stall or fall. Less shared context reduces it. Larger models hack more.
numbers: 23 seed essays; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 as author and judge; judge and author shown 1 or 3 previous iterations (four settings); three human annotators per essay, each essay graded alone. Online-judge deviation rises with iterations while human deviation does not (Figure 3).
limits: Essay editing only. Effect sizes are in figures. Abstract names context sharing and model size as the drivers.
agent_relevance: Self-written success criteria judged by the same model in the same context drift. A fixed criterion plus a judge with asymmetric context lowers drift. It did not compare a fixed criterion against a self-written one, so gap 6 is only partly closed.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: ablation studies (Section 3.4, Appendix B.3)
finding: Gap 8. In Voyager, replacing the automatic curriculum with a random one cuts discovered items by 93%. Removing self-verification cuts items by 73%. Without the skill library progress plateaus late. GPT-4 code generation gives 5.7 times more unique items than GPT-3.5.
numbers: Discovered item count in Minecraft. Random curriculum: -93%. No self-verification: -73%. GPT-3.5: 5.7x fewer items. Manual curriculum and no-skill-library are lower, shown in Figure 9 curves only.
limits: Ablations are not matched for tokens; the axis is iterations. Few runs. The curriculum is a proposal from the model's own state, not an information-gain term.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 in part: the curriculum (what to try next given current state) matters most early; the skill library (kept results) matters late; both are needed. Exploration pressure is not separated from the skill library at equal tokens.

source: Wei (2024) Value of information and reward specification in active inference and POMDPs (regret rule, not re-opened)
finding: Gap 10. Only the earlier evidence line b14 was available; the paper was not re-opened this session. No new reading of the rule that scales exploration with difficulty.
limits: Not opened this session. Bound holds for known POMDP models with a temperature parameter, not for LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: no tested rule maps problem difficulty to an exploration budget for an LLM.
